title: Having a Sweet Tooth Linked to Safer Choices
paragraphs: Do you love very sweet tastes? According to a new study from Russia, your sweet tooth may be linked to the way you make decisions about money, and surprisingly, it may make you more cautious.

The study was carried out by researchers at the Centre for Cognition and Decision Making at HSE University in Moscow, including Ksenia Panidi, and it was published in the journal Frontiers in Psychology in 2026.

To find out who had a sweet tooth, the researchers asked participants to taste five glasses of sugar water with different levels of sweetness and rate how pleasant each one was. People who liked the sweetest solution the most were classified as "sweet-likers." Previous research has suggested that this preference is partly inherited and tends to stay the same throughout life.

In the first experiment, 49 adults took part in decision-making tasks involving real money. In one task, they had to choose between receiving a guaranteed amount of money and entering a lottery in which they could win more, or nothing at all. The researchers had expected sweet-likers to take more risks. However, the opposite was true. Sweet-likers were less likely to choose the lottery and more likely to take the guaranteed money.

A second experiment, involving 100 new participants, produced a similar result, although the difference only appeared when the chances of winning the lottery were 50-50. In addition, sweet-likers were more likely to choose a smaller reward right away rather than wait for a larger one. However, the researchers found that this was partly explained by their dislike of uncertainty.
Interestingly, in another task in which participants inflated a virtual balloon to earn money, there was no difference between the groups.

The researchers suggest that the brain's opioid system, which is involved in feelings of pleasure, may influence how people value both sweet tastes and rewards. However, they did not test this directly.

The study also had limitations. The effects were small, the amounts of money involved were low and all the participants were young adults from Moscow. As Panidi pointed out, liking sweet tastes in a laboratory test is also very different from liking sweet foods in everyday life.
